title: The ghost and the curly tail
hookLine: a ghost, a dog's curly tail, and why seva still matters when the world won't change
carry: seva: serving others changes the one who serves
tomorrow: a mongoose, half gold, says a king's great sacrifice isn't enough. why?

lines: WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.
cards: A year of volunteering, donating, showing up for the cause, and the problem looks exactly the same. The shelter is still full. The inbox is still full.
And a quiet voice asks: what's the point? Vivekananda took that question seriously.

In his Karma Yoga lectures he answered it with a strange little story about a man, a ghost, and a dog's tail that would not stay straight. The chapter's title sounds almost rude: We Help Ourselves, Not the World.

teach.h: A GHOST THAT MUST BE KEPT BUSY.
teach.b: Here's the story as Vivekananda tells it. A man wanted a ghost to do his work for him, and he got one. But there was a catch: the ghost had to be kept busy every minute, or it would kill him.
It finished every job in no time. Build a house: done. Clear a field: done.

teach.h: THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.
teach.b: The man, terrified, ran to a wise teacher, who said: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail. The ghost pulled the tail straight. Let go, and it curled back up.
Pulled again. Curled. That kept it busy.
The world, Vivekananda said, is like that dog's tail. People keep pulling it straight; let go, and it curls. So is helping pointless?
No. That's the turn. When we help, he said, we're not fixing the world.
The world will go on. We are the ones being changed. So, he said, be grateful to the person you help: they gave you the chance.

teach.h: SEVA: THE HELPER IS THE ONE WHO CHANGES.
teach.b: Hindus call this kind of help seva, selfless service, and many temples run on it. And serve, he said, like a master, not a slave, the way Janaka ruled.

teach.h: A LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.
teach.b: The Gita has a picture for it: the one who acts, offering the action and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by it, the way a lotus leaf sits in water and stays dry.

teach.h: SEVA CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.
teach.b: The tail still curls. You keep straightening it anyway, and you stay dry.

how: In seva, service offered freely, many Hindus aim to help without clinging to results or credit, often using the Gita's image of the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet.

o: an expert who has perfected a craft
one who works freely, not for the reward
a boss who has others do the work for him

games.q: the story and its point — tap the pairs.

s: Vivekananda said helping others is pointless because the world won't change
he said helping is how the helper grows, and we should be grateful to the ones we help.
the Gita compares unattached action to a lotus leaf in water
Gita 5.10: offered action doesn't stain, as water doesn't wet the lotus leaf.
'work like a master, not a slave' means make others work for you
it means work freely, because the work is worth doing, not for the reward.

games.q: you've served at the temple food pantry for a year, and the line is just as long. by Vivekananda's karma yoga, what's true?
o: stop: the tail always curls back.
keep serving, unattached: seva changes the one who serves.
serve harder until the world is fixed for good.
games.why: the world is a curly tail, and the helper is the one who grows. so be grateful to the ones you serve.

practice: Think of one thing you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back: a cause, a messy house, a relative who won't change. Breathe in and feel how much you want the result; breathe out and set the result down beside you, just for now.
Then picture doing the next small piece anyway, because it's worth doing, like the lotus leaf: in the water, and dry.

wordCard.voice: Master, one who works freely, not for reward. In seva, we help ourselves, not the world: the work changes the worker. Stay dry like the lotus leaf.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 5.10: 'like a lotus leaf by water' — untouched by what it sits in.

carryVoice: Your line: seva: serving others changes the one who serves. The tail still curls, and the helper still grows. Day two hundred sixty-five, done.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga (1896), ch. 5, 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World' (the ghost and the dog's curly tail)
Bhagavad Gita 5.10 (the lotus leaf untouched by water)
